title: Recovery Is the New Rigor
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart uses a school garden metaphor — the difference between jet, mist, and shower hose settings — to argue that modern schools have been set to 'Jet': they treat education as a delivery problem (instructional minutes, standards covered, interventions administered) while almost entirely ignoring the absorption gap between what adults deliver and what children's brains, bodies, and nervous systems can actually take in, hold, and use. Using the American Academy of Pediatrics' 2026 recess guidance as a launching point, Stinehart argues that recess is not dessert but digestion: the place where learning metabolises from 'I understood that while the teacher was standing next to me' into durable, applicable knowledge. Withholding recess as punishment is a design flaw, not a discipline strategy — the children most in need of movement, peer practice, and stress regulation are consistently the first to lose it. The article ends with the proposition that 'recovery is the new rigor': genuine rigour requires designing conditions where children can sustain meaningful effort without breakdown.
points: The absorption gap is the overlooked half of the teaching equation: schools optimise delivery metrics (instructional minutes, standards covered) while paying almost no attention to whether the child's brain and body are in a state where input can become usable learning.

The AAP's 2026 recess guidance is the first in 13 years and affirms recess is crucial for health, academic success, and mental, physical, social, and emotional growth — it should never be withheld for academic or punitive reasons.

Recess is not a break from learning but digestion: the body moves, stress levels change, attention resets, and the brain consolidates what was delivered in class — removing it sabotages the very retention schools are trying to produce.

The children who most need recess are consistently the first to lose it: the child who can't sit still, talks too much, or struggles to finish work — all signs of a nervous system that needs movement — gets recess withheld, amplifying the dysregulation rather than resolving it.

Recess is an equity issue: children from resource-rich families can recover lost autonomy and play through other channels; children for whom school is the safest, most reliable environment have no substitute when recess is taken away.
quotes: For decades, we have treated education like a delivery problem. Did we deliver the lesson? Did we cover the standard? Did we administer the assessment? Did we provide the intervention? Those questions matter. But they are incomplete, because learning is not delivery. Learning is intake.
What if we are not under-instructing children? What if we are over-blasting them? What if some learning does not stick because the school day gives children almost no time for it to settle?
Recess is not what happens after learning. Recess is where learning goes to metabolize so it can be put to use. The break is not empty. The break is where the absorption happens.

For years, schools have confused rigor with endurance. A school day that ignores how children actually develop is not rigorous. It is just stubborn. Real rigor is not seeing how long a child can sit before their nervous system starts filing a formal complaint.

The children showing the clearest signs that they need movement, peer practice, stress relief, and self-regulation opportunities are often the children most likely to have those things removed. That is not discipline. That is a design flaw.

The playground conflicts are not always a distraction from learning. Sometimes they are the learning. We keep saying children need collaboration, communication, resilience, self-regulation, creativity, empathy, leadership, and problem-solving. Then we remove the one part of the school day where those things happen.
